Last time I tried to jump start a battery with another car (running) but it failed. Now I see this youtube clip and wonder why last time it did not start my car.

How to Jump-Start a Car Battery:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GQaMn_85VQU

The biggest difference is probably that last time I connected the "+" to the "+" and the "-" to the "-". While in this clip I must connect the "-" to the metal chassis of the car that needs jump starting.

The question is why?

Edit: Based on the feedback I get it daunts me. We are not talking about small current like 1 amperes but a massive current 500+ amperes for a short moment.

  • When I connect it to the "-" part of the battery then first the empty battery will eat up the negative incoming charge, but also the electrons gets a bottleneck on the cable from the negative charge to the started motor. Losing voltage.
  • Using the metal chassis of the car I have a huge metal conducting surface that leads directly to the starter motor. And the empty battery can't suck up so many electrons because the negative cable is is creating a traffic jam; So more electrons that moves to the starter motor.

Electrons move from the negative side (because they are negative ans has too much electrone) toward the positive side (that has a lack of electrons).
Jump-Start a Car Battery: Why must the "-" be connected to a metal mass?

There is no need to do it this way, but the minus pole of car batteries are connected to the chassis. That way when jumpstarting a common zero point is present and the plus pole of the battery will be 12 volts more.

Because you are'nt trying to charge the batrery with your jump car.

You are trying to direct all the jump car's juice to the starter motor of the dead car so you go around the battery.

You dont need to do this, but putting the ground wire (-) closer to the starter will make the circuit better for the starter. If you just ground battery to battery you are grounding everything in the car through the battery and the starter sometimes cant get enough juice to turn over fast enough.

I don't know why but I've always had a hard time understanding electricity. Why aren't car chassis's electrically charged if the (-) is connected to it without the car having any solid connection to the ground?
The battery has both a + and - side that has an equal charge, so the average of the car equals to zero.

Funny enough, the signs for positive and negative for cars are backwards of normal electrical theory. If the positive is connected without a ground technically the chassis is charged. But grounding it closer to whatever component you are trying to use will always make a better circuit because there is less distance the charge will have to travel back to the power source.

It really depends on the vehicle. I've had vehicles start with the negative jumper hooked to the battery, but not start with it hooked to the engine or body, and vice versa. The goal is to get the negative jumper hooked to the cleanest ground possible, and there is an abundance of places to do that on most vehicles.

The best explanation I've heard for this is that the car's starter motor (where most of the amps draw is going) is connected to ground by direct contact to the chassis. (It's bolted onto the engine block.) Connecting the negative to the frame allows the most direct (least resistance) current path to the starter. The positive is still running through a wire, but total resistance is still lower.
